title: When the answer doesn't work: correcting course
promise: You'll know how to write the exact correction for the four classic failures — generic, too long, too short, or made up — and get the good answer on the second try instead of the ninth.
why: Marta has a plant shop in Ruzafa and asked ChatGPT for the "Shipping and returns" section of her website. She got back 900 words that would work just as well for a plant shop as for a tire shop, so she wrote "I don't like it, make it better" and got another 900 equally empty ones back. Forty minutes and five tries later she was in the same place. The failure wasn't the model's: "make it better" doesn't carry a single clue about what was wrong, and this lesson is the repertoire of phrases that do.

theory.title: "Make it better" isn't a correction
theory.text: The AI can't see your face. When you read its answer and something bugs you, you know exactly what it is; it has no way of finding out. A correction only works if it carries new information, and the formula that works has three parts: what part is wrong, why it's wrong for your specific case, and what you want instead. Skip the third and the AI guesses again, and guessing is exactly what it already got wrong the first time. There's also a detail that changes the result a lot: don't criticize the whole answer, point at the piece. Select the eight or ten words that bother you with your mouse and paste them into your message in quotes. That turns a complaint into an instruction, and an instruction can actually be executed.
theory.analogy: It's like sending a dish back at a restaurant. "It's bad" makes the waiter shrug and take it away with no idea what to tell the cook. "The pasta is undercooked, I want it five more minutes" comes back from the kitchen fixed.
theory.example: Bad: "I'm not convinced, improve it." Good: "Where it says 'we're committed to offering quality service,' cut it entirely: that's brochure language and I sell plants to people who just want to know when their monstera arrives. Put the real timeframe there instead: 48-72 hours mainland, 5 days to the islands."

theory.title: Four failures with four different causes
theory.text: Almost every bad answer falls into four buckets: generic, too long, too short, or made up. From the inside they all feel the same — "this doesn't work for me" — but they come from different places and get fixed with different phrasing. Generic means you gave it nothing of yours, so it handed you back the average of everything it's ever read. Long means you didn't give it a cap, and by default it tends to fill until it feels like a complete piece. Short usually means you didn't tell it how deep to go, and it stopped at the headline. Made up means you asked it for a fact it doesn't have and didn't give it permission to say "I don't know." Before writing a single word of the correction, decide which bucket you're in: correcting the wrong bucket is what makes the second try come out as bad as the first.

theory.title: Generic: it's missing something of yours
theory.text: A language model (the program behind ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini) works by predicting what would come next after what's in front of it. If your request would apply to ten thousand businesses, the prediction applies to ten thousand businesses too. That's why "write me the pricing section for my website" always sounds like a template: you've described a gap, not a business. The fix isn't asking for more creativity or more punch, it's feeding it data. Three to five concrete facts of yours — numbers, names, the neighborhood, what customers actually tell you — change the answer far more than any adjective you tack on. And there's a trick that doubles the effect: give it an example of what you DON'T want and one of what you do, even if you write the good one badly. What you write clumsily carries information that what it writes well doesn't have.
theory.example: Marta swapped "write me the shipping policy" for this: "I ship from Valencia with Correos Express. 48-72 h mainland, 5 days to the Balearics, I don't ship to the Canaries. Free shipping over €45, otherwise €4.90. Plants travel with the root ball wrapped in film. If a leaf arrives broken I send a replacement, if the plant arrives dead I refund the full amount. Write that in 150 words, casual tone, don't use the word commitment." Usable answer on the first try.

theory.title: Too long or too short: numbers measure, adjectives don't
theory.text: "Shorter" is an opinion, "maximum 120 words" is an instruction. Models follow numeric caps reasonably well and almost never adjectives, so always give it a unit you can check at a glance: words, sentences, list items, lines. When the answer's too long, there's almost always a twenty percent inside that's actually good, so don't throw the whole thing out: tell it what stays and what goes, and forbid it from touching what stays. With short answers there's a trap that trips up almost everyone. A lot of the time what's missing isn't more words, it's more depth, and those are two different things. Ask for "longer" and you get the same idea stretched with filler; ask "explain point 3 as if I had to do it tomorrow morning, including what could go wrong," and you get something completely different.
theory.analogy: Asking for "shorter" is like telling a tailor "take it up." He takes it up an inch or a foot, however he feels, and you come back another day. "Two centimeters above the ankle" only has one possible reading.

theory.title: It made it up, and why you shouldn't ask if it's sure
theory.text: This is called a hallucination, and it's not some rare glitch: it's its normal way of working seen from the bad side. The model always produces the most plausible continuation, and plausible and true look a lot alike but aren't the same thing. It doesn't know it's making things up; to it, a law that exists and a law that sounds like it exists are written with the same ease. That's why the worst question you can ask it is "are you sure?" That checks nothing: it only pushes it to agree with you, and it often backs off on a fact that was correct just because it noticed you doubting. What does work is asking it to separate what it knows from what it's assuming, to mark each claim with its confidence level, and to tell you where to verify it. Proper names, figures, dates, laws, prices, links, and direct quotes always get checked outside, against the original source, no exceptions.
theory.example: The made-up link is the most common case and the easiest to catch: if it gives you a URL (a web page address), open it. If the site doesn't exist, or if it drops you on the homepage instead of the page it claimed, the rest of that answer deserves exactly the same distrust.

theory.title: When to stop correcting and start over
theory.text: Everything written in a chat keeps weighing on what comes after, including the three bad answers you've already dismissed. If you've corrected three times and the problem hasn't budged, you're no longer correcting: you're piling up junk that drags the conversation somewhere you don't want to go. The tell is unmistakable: the fourth answer looks more like the first than like what you just asked for. There are two ways out. The fast one: in ChatGPT and Claude you can edit your own message — hover over it and a pencil appears — and editing it rebuilds the conversation from that point, so the bad answer stops counting. The good one: open a new chat and start it with everything you've learned folded into the first message, including what you already tried that didn't work. Editing your message doesn't delete anything from your account: it creates a branch, and you can go back to the previous one with the little arrows that appear next to it.
theory.analogy: It's like straightening out a conversation with someone who misunderstood from minute one. Past a certain point it's cheaper to say "wait, let me start over" than to keep qualifying on top of qualifications.

tasks.title: Provoke a generic answer on purpose
tasks.where: In the ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini app, in a new chat
tasks.action: Click "New chat" (top left, the paper-and-pencil icon) and paste the request below exactly as it is, without adding anything of your own. This is on purpose: you want to see a generic answer up close so you can spot one in two seconds from now on. When it arrives, read only the first sentence of each paragraph.
tasks.prompt: Write the "About us" section for my business's website. Make it convey trust and professionalism.
tasks.expect: Between 200 and 500 words that would work just as well for a hair salon, an accounting firm, or a bike shop. Words that will almost certainly show up: passion, commitment, quality, our team, the customer at the center. Not a single fact that's actually yours, because you didn't give it any.
tasks.stuck: If instead of text it asks you questions (Claude does this often), reply "doesn't matter, make it up" and you now have your generic answer. That's exactly the material you need for the next exercise.

tasks.title: Correct it with the three-part formula
tasks.where: In the same chat, right below that answer
tasks.action: Don't write "make it better." Select the emptiest sentence in the whole answer with your mouse — the one that would fit any business — and paste it into the message below, where it asks. Also fill in the four facts with real details from your project. If you don't have a business yet, use one you know well: the bakery on your street works fine.
tasks.prompt:
I'm going to correct this answer and I want you to apply the full correction, not a tweak.

WHAT'S WRONG: this sentence of yours — "[PASTE THE EMPTIEST SENTENCE FROM ITS ANSWER HERE]" — and everything else in the same style. It would fit any business in the world, so it says nothing about mine.

WHY IT'S WRONG FOR MY CASE: my customers don't choose based on "professionalism," they choose because of [WHAT ACTUALLY MAKES THEM BUY FROM YOU].

WHAT I WANT INSTEAD: the same text, written using only these facts of mine:
- [FACT 1: how long you've been around and where you're located]
- [FACT 2: a real number: customers, years, kilos, orders, whatever]
- [FACT 3: something you do differently from the shop next door]
- [FACT 4: something a real customer of yours has actually said]

RULES: maximum 150 words. Casual tone. These words are banned: passion, commitment, quality, excellence, our team, industry leaders. If you're missing a fact, leave it in brackets instead of making it up. Don't explain what you did: just give me the text.
tasks.expect: A text under 150 words where you recognize your business as you read it. If a banned word sneaks back in, flag it with "you used 'commitment,' remove it" and that's it: that short back-and-forth is normal, not a sign you're doing it wrong.
tasks.stuck: If it still sounds like a template, the problem is your four facts, not the correction. Swap them for more uncomfortable ones to write: the exact price, the neighborhood's name, the mistake you made last year. The more specific and slightly embarrassing, the better the text comes out.

tasks.title: Confirm that numbers win and adjectives don't
tasks.action: You're going to see it with your own eyes in two minutes. Send the first message and count the words by eye (a line on your phone is about 10 words, a line on a computer about 15). Then send the second message in that same chat and compare the two results.
tasks.prompt:
MESSAGE 1 (send this alone):
Explain in a few words what a web domain is.

MESSAGE 2 (send this after, in the same chat):
Now the same thing again, but with these exact rules: maximum 60 words, three sentences, no examples, no intro, no closing sentence. Start directly with "A domain is".
tasks.expect: The first answer will run 150-250 words, with its intro and its sign-off. The second will fit entirely on screen without scrolling and will start where you told it to. If you count and get 63 words instead of 60, that's fine: the cap is a target, not a contract.
tasks.stuck: If the second one still comes out long, you asked for too many things at once. Leave it with just "maximum 60 words" and drop the other rules: caps get followed much better on their own.

tasks.title: Rescue a long answer without regenerating it
tasks.where: In any chat where you have an answer that's too long
tasks.action: Find a long answer you already have handy; the one from exercise 1 works. Don't ask it to summarize, because a summary drags the good parts down with it too. Tell it what stays, what goes, and explicitly forbid it from touching what stays.
tasks.prompt:
Don't rewrite this answer: trim it.

KEEP EXACTLY: [WHICH PARTS ARE ACTUALLY GOOD, e.g. "the first three paragraphs and the final list"].
DELETE: everything else, especially the intro, the general context, the sentences about how important the topic is, and the conclusion.

TRIMMING RULES:
- Don't touch what stays. Not a different word, not a synonym, nothing "improved along the way."
- If removing something leaves a sentence hanging, join it to the next one, but without adding new ideas.
- Give me only the final text. Below it, on a single line, tell me how many words it had before and how many it has now.
tasks.expect: The trimmed text, with the sentences you liked exactly as they were, and a line like "before 480 words, now 190." Check one thing: the sentences you said should stay have to be identical, word for word.
tasks.stuck: If it rewrote them "along the way," say so: "You changed paragraph 2. Give it back to me word for word as it was and apply only the deletions." It's the most common mistake and it almost always gets fixed on the first warning.

tasks.title: Turn a short answer into a deep one, not a long one
tasks.action: Ask it something deliberately vague: "how do I get my first customers?" You'll get a list of six one-line points, all true and all useless. Now, instead of asking for "longer," pick ONE point from that list and send the message below with its number.
tasks.prompt:
I want the long version of point [NUMBER] from your list. Nothing else from the rest.

Write it as if I had to do it tomorrow morning and had never done anything like it. Include:
1. Exactly what I do on day one, step by step, with the real names of things and what to click.
2. How much it costs in dollars, and whether there's a free way to do it, and what that is.
3. How long until I know if it's working.
4. The two mistakes people starting out with this make most.
5. How I know I've done it right and how I know I've done it wrong.

No general theory. If something depends on my specific situation, ask me instead of assuming.
tasks.expect: An answer considerably longer than the first, but full of instructions you can follow tomorrow, not sentences about how important getting customers is. It's very likely to also ask you one or two questions at the end.
tasks.stuck: If it goes back to generalities, the point you picked was too big ("do marketing"). Pick a much smaller one: "write the exact WhatsApp message I send to a customer who hasn't bought from me in a year."

tasks.title: Catch a fabrication with the confidence traffic light
tasks.action: Ask it something where it's easy for it to make things up, meaning something with names and numbers. For example: "What obligations does an online store in the US have around return rights, and what exact deadline does the law set?" When it answers, do NOT ask if it's sure. Paste this.
tasks.prompt:
Go through your previous answer and classify every claim you made into one of these three:

GREEN — something stable and widely repeated, very unlikely to be wrong.
AMBER — likely, but you're not certain of it: it could have changed or depend on the specific case.
RED — a concrete fact (a law's name, an article number, a figure, a date, a price, a link) you wrote because it fit, not because you've verified it.

Give it back as a list: claim, color, and on one line, where I'd check it (the name of the agency or official publication, not a link).

Don't change your answer. Don't add new information. And don't apologize: I just want the traffic light.
tasks.expect: A list where several things land on amber or red, especially the legal citations and deadlines. That's exactly what you wanted to see. The useful answer isn't the one that's all green, it's the one that tells you where you need to look yourself.
tasks.stuck: If it marks everything green, it's siding with you. Push back with: "The specific article you cited — do you actually have it, or did you construct it? Answer only 'I have it' or 'I constructed it.'" Then check it yourself on the official site. A legal deadline or a price is never taken as good just because a chat said so: if you publish a wrong return deadline on your site, you're the one who answers for it.

tasks.title: Armor the question before you ask it
tasks.where: In a new chat, as the very first message
tasks.action: This is preventive mode and it saves roughly half your corrections. It gets pasted BEFORE asking anything. Send it, wait for confirmation, and then ask your actual question in that same chat.
tasks.prompt:
Before I ask you anything, I want to set how you have to answer me for the rest of this conversation. Five rules:

1. If you don't know something, say so. "I don't know" is an answer I'll happily accept. Making up a fact to fill a gap is the one mistake I won't forgive.
2. Proper names, figures, dates, laws, prices, and links: only if you actually have them. If not, write [UNCONFIRMED] right after and keep going.
3. No intros, no closing summaries, and no telling me my question is very interesting. Start directly with the answer.
4. I'm not a programmer. Translate any technical word in parentheses the first time you use it.
5. If my question can't be answered well without a fact I haven't given you, ask me instead of assuming. I'd rather get a question from you than a half answer.

Respond now with only "done" and any doubts you have about these rules. Don't write anything else.
tasks.expect: A short "done," at most with one question after it. If it gives you three paragraphs explaining how great it thinks the rules are, it's not applying them: reply "rule 3" and you'll see the change.
tasks.stuck: If later in that same conversation it slips back into old habits, don't repeat all five rules. Just write "rule 2" or "rule 3." It works because they're written earlier in the chat and it still has them in view.

tasks.title: Edit your message instead of writing another one
tasks.where: In the ChatGPT or Claude app, over a message you already sent
tasks.action: Find a message of YOURS in your conversation that triggered a bad answer. Hover over it; on mobile, press and hold. A pencil or an "Edit" button appears. Click it, fix your message by adding what it was missing, and hit "Send." The conversation rebuilds from that point, so the bad answer stops being in the middle and stops dragging on what comes next.
tasks.expect: The bad answer disappears from view and a new one arrives. Right above or below the message you'll see something like "1/2" with two small arrows: those are the two versions. Nothing gets deleted from your account, and you can go back to the previous one with the left arrow whenever you want.
tasks.stuck: If you can't find the pencil: in Gemini the button is in the corner of the message and sometimes only shows on the last one you sent. If your app doesn't have it, no problem, do task 9: get the same result a different way.

tasks.title: Restart a poisoned chat with a handoff
tasks.where: In a chat that's had three corrections in a row with no improvement
tasks.action: Before abandoning it, extract what you've learned from it. Paste the message below into the old chat, copy what it gives you back, open a new chat, and paste it as the first message. You're taking what's useful and leaving behind the three bad answers that were weighing the conversation down.
tasks.prompt:
Let's leave this conversation here. But first, write me the message I'll use to start a new conversation about the same thing, so I don't start from zero.

That message needs to include, in this order:
1. What I'm trying to achieve, in two sentences, with my specific details.
2. My facts that I've given you throughout this conversation, as a list. All of them, even ones that seem minor.
3. The decisions we've already made that don't need revisiting.
4. What we've tried here that did NOT work, with one line explaining why.
5. The formatting rules I want followed.
6. The exact question that needs solving now.

Write it in second person, addressed to the AI, ready to copy and paste. Keep it under 300 words. Don't add anything we haven't discussed here.
tasks.expect: A block of text you can copy in full. Read it before pasting: if you see any fact you never gave it, remove it, because it just made that up right there. Point 4 is the most valuable, because it's what stops the new chat from repeating the same mistake.
tasks.stuck: If the handoff comes out huge or repetitive, tell it: "Trim it to 200 words by cutting anything that doesn't change any decision." And if the old chat is so lost that even the handoff comes out wrong, write it yourself by hand in five lines: it's still far better than starting from a blank page.

matters: Diagnosing before correcting. If you write the correction without deciding which of the four buckets you're in (generic, long, short, made up), the second try comes out just as bad as the first and you'll have spent two rounds staying exactly where you started.

Numbers instead of adjectives. "Shorter," "more professional," and "more punch" can't be followed or checked; "120 words," "three sentences," and "no using the word commitment" can. Every loose adjective you leave in a request is an extra round of corrections you'll pay for later.

Verifying externally any fact with a name or number attached: laws, deadlines, prices, articles, links, people's names. Publishing a made-up legal deadline on your site isn't an AI failure, it's your website and your responsibility, and a badly written return policy costs you in dollars and complaints.

Knowing when to stop. Three corrections with no progress means the chat is weighed down and it's time to open a new one with a handoff. The people who really get stuck aren't the ones who write weak requests, they're the ones who push twelve times in the same chat hoping the thirteenth will be different.
ignore: Temperature, top-p, and the other tuning dials. They show up in tutorials written by people coding against the API (the back door through which a program talks to the AI without going through the app). Inside the app you don't have them and don't need them for any of this.

Picking the perfect model. Switching from ChatGPT to Claude doesn't fix a badly written correction. Once you actually know how to correct, you'll notice the real difference between them; right now it just distracts from what actually changes the result.

The mile-long prompts floating around the internet, with fifty rules, capital letters, and emojis. A good chunk of those rules contradict each other and the model ends up obeying whichever came last. You're better served by the five rules in task 7.
canDo: Trim a text while literally respecting what you tell it not to touch, if you ask it in those exact words and forbid "improving along the way."
Meet numeric caps: words, sentences, list items. It lands close rather than hitting it exactly, and for what you need, that's enough.
Rewrite the same idea in different registers as many times as needed, without getting tired or offended. You can ask for ten versions in a row and the tenth will be as good as the first.
Separate what it knows from what it's assuming and mark it, if you ask explicitly and don't leave it the easy out of just agreeing with you.
cantDo: Know what bothered you if you don't tell it. It can't read your face, it can't see your website, and it doesn't remember the standard you used last week in a different chat.
Check on its own whether a fact is true. It can suspect a link sounds off, but it can't open it unless you have web search turned on, and even then, deciding what gets published is on you.
Hold course indefinitely in a long chat. The more text piles up above, the more the old answers weigh on it, and the further it drifts from what you asked at the start.

Change one thing without touching what's next to it. Every rewrite touches more than it should unless you put the limit in writing, which is why you always tell it what NOT to touch, not just what to change.
words: The message you write to the AI. Everything you put in the text box before hitting send, nothing more, nothing less.

Everything the AI has in front of it at the moment it answers: your current message plus everything written earlier in that same chat. That's why a bad answer keeps weighing on things even when you ignore it.
The maximum size of what fits in a conversation. Once it fills up, the oldest parts start falling off and the AI stops keeping in mind what you told it at the start.
When the AI makes up a fact with total confidence. It's not lying to you on purpose: it writes what fits well, and what fits well sometimes doesn't exist.
Improving something round by round. You ask, look at what comes out, correct one specific thing, look again. Two or three rounds is normal; twelve is a warning sign.
Asking it to answer the same message again, to see if it comes out better. It's the two-circling-arrows button below the answer.
The small chunk the AI splits text into so it can read it. It's roughly three quarters of a word, which is why size limits get counted in odd ways.
The AI's tendency to agree with you. If you ask "are you sure?", it often backs down even when it was right, just because it noticed you doubting.
next: In the next lesson you build your own request template, with your data already baked in, so most of these corrections stop being necessary.
